{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-mo-f","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"1cd6d1fea49f63d7227b9dab1c6c806d494cef0307de3445a833ce7cabe9b3e4","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-mo-class-f:lineage:41","source_registry_sha256":"f128002157e581eb7004b9370c8cfbafd7b29a1596262980704fbda0a45932f5","source_liveness_sha256":"fdf72d02e75b9589fee5aaf5b83ec9705ff03586f574464e3553a827f9b698d8"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Missouri everyday safe driving: seat belts and child restraints, defensive driving, posture and steering, following distance, space cushions, stopping distance, signaling, horn use, slow driving, carbon monoxide, deer crashes, tires and traffic stops","heading":"C — Everyday safe driving: seat belt and child restraint law, air bags, defensive driving, posture and steering grip, the three second rule, space behind and beside you, stopping distance, signaling, horn use, slow driving, carbon monoxide, deer, tire checks and what to do at a traffic stop","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Everyday safe driving: seat belt and child restraint law, air bags, defensive driving, posture and steering grip, the three second rule, space behind and beside you, stopping distance, signaling, horn use, slow driving, carbon monoxide, deer, tire checks and what to do at a traffic stop
Knowledge domain: who must buckle up and how child passengers are restrained by age, weight and height, why air bags do not replace belts, how to drive defensively and hold the wheel, how to keep space ahead, behind and beside you, what makes up stopping distance, how and when to signal and use the horn, the law on driving too slowly, how to avoid carbon monoxide and deer crashes, how to check tires, and how to behave during a traffic stop.

FACT_ID: sec10-F01 | anchor: A01
Buckle your own seat belt before driving and make sure every passenger uses a belt or child restraint, because belts greatly cut the chance of injury or death in a crash. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec10-F02 | anchor: A01
Wear the lap belt low and snug across the hips with the shoulder belt across the chest, never under the arm or behind the back, and use both parts of a two-part belt. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec10-F03 | anchor: A01
Wear a belt even with air bags, since air bags do not protect you in side or rear impacts or rollovers and will not keep you behind the wheel. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec10-F04 | anchor: A01
A deploying air bag can seriously hurt or kill someone who is unbelted or badly belted, and NHTSA advises at least ten inches between the center of the breastbone and the steering wheel hub. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec10-F05 | anchor: A01
Children 12 and under should always ride properly restrained in a back seat, and a rear-facing infant seat must never go in front of an active passenger air bag. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec10-F06 | anchor: A01
Missouri law requires the driver and front seat passengers of every passenger vehicle to wear a properly adjusted, fastened seat belt. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec10-F07 | anchor: A01
When an intermediate license holder is driving, every passenger in the vehicle must be properly restrained. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec10-F08 | anchor: A01
A child under four years old must ride in a suitable child restraint system no matter how much the child weighs. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec10-F09 | anchor: A01
A child weighing under 40 pounds must ride in a suitable child restraint system no matter how old the child is. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec10-F10 | anchor: A02
A child aged four to under eight who weighs from 40 to under 80 pounds and is shorter than 4 feet 9 inches must ride in a child restraint system or booster seat. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec10-F11 | anchor: A02
A child who is at least eight, at least 80 pounds, or taller than 4 feet 9 inches must use a vehicle safety belt or a suitable booster seat. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec10-F12 | anchor: A02
Defensive drivers keep their eyes moving ahead, to the sides and behind through the mirrors every few seconds, and watch oncoming traffic, since distracted drivers crossing the center line cause many head-on crashes. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec10-F13 | anchor: A02
Expect other drivers to make mistakes, such as not stopping at a stop sign, plan how you would react, and never cause a crash on purpose even when someone fails to yield. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec10-F14 | anchor: A02
Do not count on signals or signs to stop others from crossing your path; look left and right at intersections even when cross traffic faces a red light or stop sign. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec10-F15 | anchor: A02
Hold the wheel with your left hand between the seven and nine o'clock positions and your right hand between three and five o'clock. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec10-F16 | anchor: A02
Steer around corners with the hand-over-hand method rather than palming the wheel with one hand, and straighten the wheel by hand after the turn. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec10-F17 | anchor: A03
Never turn the ignition key to the lock position while the vehicle is moving, because the steering wheel will lock when you turn it and you will lose control. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec10-F18 | anchor: A03
Rear-end crashes are very common and are caused by drivers following so closely that they cannot stop when the car ahead stops suddenly. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec10-F19 | anchor: A03
Under the three second rule, start counting when the car ahead passes a fixed object, and if you reach the object before you count to three, you are too close. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec10-F20 | anchor: A03
Help the driver behind keep a safe gap by holding a steady speed and signaling early before you slow down. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec10-F21 | anchor: A03
If a tailgater follows you and there is a right lane, move into it; if not, wait for clear road and slow down gradually, never braking suddenly. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec10-F22 | anchor: A03
Avoid driving alongside other vehicles on multi-lane roads, keep away from oncoming traffic by not crowding the center line, and generally stay in the middle of your lane. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec10-F23 | anchor: A04
Give pedestrians and cyclists, especially children, extra room, and take hazards one at a time, for example letting an oncoming car pass before you overtake a cyclist. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec10-F24 | anchor: A04
Stopping distance is reaction distance plus braking distance, and speed, fatigue or poor brakes all increase it. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec10-F25 | anchor: A04
Reaction distance is how far you travel between seeing a danger and braking, and the guide's chart assumes a reaction time of 1.5 seconds. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec10-F26 | anchor: A04
Braking distance is how far you travel from applying the brakes to a full stop, and the chart assumes good brakes, tires, weather and road. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec10-F27 | anchor: A04
Signal before changing lanes, turning, merging or parking, and do it every time you change direction even if no one seems to be around. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec10-F28 | anchor: A04
Signal at least 100 feet ahead, but if streets, driveways or entrances lie between you and your turn, wait until you pass them before signaling. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec10-F29 | anchor: A05
After a turn or lane change make sure the signal has shut off, because a signal left blinking can make others think you will turn again. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec10-F30 | anchor: A05
The only reason to sound your horn is to warn other drivers, and needless honking can distract others and cause a crash. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec10-F31 | anchor: A05
Driving below a posted minimum speed in normal conditions is illegal, though bad weather, heavy traffic or a bad road can justify going slower. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec10-F32 | anchor: A05
Even with no posted minimum, it is illegal to drive so slowly that you block traffic, and if vehicles line up behind you, pull over and let them pass. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec10-F33 | anchor: A05
Avoid carbon monoxide by never running the engine in a garage or in a parked car with the windows shut, including running the heater or air conditioner. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec10-F34 | anchor: A05
Deer rarely travel alone, so if you see one crossing or a struck deer by the road, expect more nearby, especially near fields, streams and gardens. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec10-F35 | anchor: A05
Most deer crashes happen in January, May and October through December, and the riskiest times are sunset to midnight and around sunrise. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec10-F36 | anchor: A05
At night with no oncoming traffic, use high beams, which light up the eyes of deer near the road and give you more time to react. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec10-F37 | anchor: A06
If hitting a deer cannot be avoided, do not swerve, because leaving the road or crossing into oncoming traffic raises the risk of injury. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec10-F38 | anchor: A06
After a deer crash, report it to local law enforcement, get a police report if your insurer needs one, and tell a local Department of Conservation agent where it happened. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec10-F39 | anchor: A06
For the penny test, put Lincoln's head into the lowest groove; if part of his head is covered, the tread is safe, and below about 2/32 of an inch grip in bad conditions drops sharply. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec10-F40 | anchor: A06
When emergency lights appear behind you, stay calm, signal, and pull off or to the side as soon as it is safe. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec10-F41 | anchor: A06
Once stopped, turn off the engine and radio, stay inside unless told to get out, keep your hands on the wheel, and do not use phones or search for documents until the officer asks. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec10-F42 | anchor: A06
If there is a weapon in the vehicle, tell the officer when the officer first makes contact. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec10-F43 | anchor: A07
Signing a traffic ticket is not an admission of guilt, but refusing to sign it may lead to arrest; contest it in court rather than arguing at the roadside. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0063]

Misconceptions: air bags do not replace seat belts; signing a ticket is not admitting guilt; slower is not always safer, and blocking traffic by driving too slowly is illegal; braking hard to warn off a tailgater raises your crash risk.
Mnemonics: one-thousand one, one-thousand two, one-thousand three for the following gap; reaction plus braking equals stopping.
Glossary: child passenger restraint system means a car seat sized for a young child; booster seat means a raised seat that positions an adult belt on a child; reaction distance means the distance covered before you brake; braking distance means the distance covered while braking to a stop; hand-over-hand means a steering method crossing one hand over the other; tailgating means following another vehicle too closely.
Dynamic facts: the child restraint thresholds and seat belt rules are statutory and can change, deer crash timing reflects seasonal patterns stated in the guide, and agency phone numbers and web pages for child seat help may change.
